verses.text: Again, on the day when the God’s sons came to present themselves before Yahweh, Satan came also among them to present himself before Yahweh.
Yahweh said to Satan, “Where have you come from?” Satan answered Yahweh, and said, “From going back and forth in the earth, and from walking up and down in it.”

Yahweh said to Satan, “Have you considered my servant Job? For there is no one like him in the earth, a blameless and an upright man, one who fears God, and turns away from evil. He still maintains his integrity, although you incited me against him, to ruin him without cause.”
Satan answered Yahweh, and said, “Skin for skin. Yes, all that a man has he will give for his life.
But stretch out your hand now, and touch his bone and his flesh, and he will renounce you to your face.”
Yahweh said to Satan, “Behold, he is in your hand. Only spare his life.”
So Satan went out from the presence of Yahweh, and struck Job with painful sores from the sole of his foot to his head.
He took for himself a potsherd to scrape himself with, and he sat among the ashes.
Then his wife said to him, “Do you still maintain your integrity? Renounce God, and die.”
But he said to her, “You speak as one of the foolish women would speak. What? Shall we receive good at the hand of God, and shall we not receive evil?” In all this Job didn’t sin with his lips.

Now when Job’s three friends heard of all this evil that had come on him, they each came from his own place: Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Naamathite; and they made an appointment together to come to sympathize with him and to comfort him.
When they lifted up their eyes from a distance, and didn’t recognize him, they raised their voices, and wept; and they each tore his robe, and sprinkled dust on their heads toward the sky.
So they sat down with him on the ground seven days and seven nights, and no one spoke a word to him, for they saw that his grief was very great.

footnotes.content: The heavenly court gathers again—this time Satan returns with a fresh accusation. I notice how the Lord permits the accuser to come, unafraid of what he might say. There's a strength in God that doesn't fear scrutiny.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Satan claims he's been roaming the earth, seeing all. But his summary is hollow—he walks up and down, seeing much, understanding nothing. The truly observant eye is one that sees as God sees, with love beneath the looking.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Here the Lord commends Job's integrity explicitly—'he still maintains it'—even knowing Satan meant harm. This is a word of grace spoken into the heavens: God sees faithfulness, marks it, and says so. The accusation failed; the righteous one stood.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'Skin for skin'—Satan's gambit is crude: comfort is all anyone truly values, he says. But listen: he must ask permission first. He can only work within the boundaries the Lord sets. Even at his most confident, the accuser is bounded.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Satan bets everything on this: touch Job's flesh, and he'll curse God to His face. He thinks suffering unmakes faith. But he doesn't know—no one truly knows until tested—whether the human heart clings to its Maker beyond comfort and ease.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Lord consents, but marks one boundary: 'Spare his life.' Even in permission, there is a fence. God is not indifferent; He limits the trial. This sets the whole story's frame—Job will suffer, yes, but not unto death, and never beyond what the Lord allows.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Satan strikes swiftly—painful sores from foot to head. Suffering is democratic; it touches the whole person. What interests me is that Job doesn't flee, doesn't hide. He endures where he stands, and that steadfastness is itself the witness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A potsherd to scrape, the ashes to sit in—these are signs of mourning and destitution. Job descends into the appearance of the cursed. Yet even in this, he has not moved from his integrity. Outer darkness and inner faithfulness can coexist.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: His wife, in her despair, speaks what Satan could not make him speak: a curse. She sees his agony and cannot bear it, so she urges him to renounce God and end it. Her words are born of love's breaking point, yet they voice the very temptation he must refuse.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Job's answer—'Shall we receive good from God and not evil?'—is the hinge on which all his faithfulness turns. He accepts that life from God's hand carries both joy and sorrow, and he won't trade his God for comfort. The note is plain: even here, 'Job didn't sin with his lips.'
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Three friends come from distant places—Eliphaz, Bildad, Zophar—a true fellowship of the afflicted. Their journey and their resolve to 'sympathize and comfort' shows what love looks like: showing up, showing up, showing up again when sorrow is too great for words.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They don't recognize him at first—that's how far the suffering has marked him. When they do, they weep and tear their robes, sprinkle dust on their heads. These are ancient rituals of lament. They honor his sorrow with their bodies, not yet with their words.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo in their silence: sometimes the truest comfort is sitting with sorrow, saying nothing, letting another know they are not alone in the dark. These three understood this, and in that understanding, they were nearer to wisdom than they would be when they opened their mouths.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
